new_statements.quote: Similarly, this work substantiates that tone is contrastive and is not perfectly predictable. Therefore, this work accordingly categorizes Dauro as a tone language particularly a register tone language which uses two level tones; high and low that are realized as raising and falling pitch across words. At surface level, tone in the language follows the same pattern as the first tone. To be exact, at surface level a high tone persists high while a low tone keeps itself low throughout the word. [p. 59, on earlier work:] Allan (1976: 332) says that “while there are two levels of systematic pitch in [Dauro], for the most part, pitch is predictable and non-contrastive.”

new_statements.rule_in_words: The only dedicated phonology of Dawro treats word prosody as tone, not stress: two level tones (H, L) that spread over the whole word (all-high vs all-low words), contrastive both lexically (k'eesaa 'priest' vs k'éesáa 'colostrum'; matsaa 'milk' vs mátsáa 'bee') and grammatically (zoɁo 'red' vs zóɁó 'red things'). No statement about a stressed syllable is made anywhere in the thesis. Earlier work disagrees on whether pitch is contrastive: Allan 1976 (two systematic pitch levels, mostly predictable, non-contrastive), Siseraw 1989 (distinctive H/L, most words ending L).
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress. Tariku notes tone is 'not perfectly predictable'; Alebachew 2010:10 (citing Hiwot 1988:22 and Hirut 2007:99) reports that imperative/jussive verbs carry high pitch on the final syllable, and Siseraw 1989 that most words end in a low tone.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level; citation forms elicited in isolation from highland (Gok'a) dialect speakers. Related Ometo languages (Wolaitta, Gamo, Zayse, Haro) are analysed by Azeb Amha, Hayward and Hirut 2004 as tone-accent languages with one H per word; Tariku's whole-word H/L analysis of Dawro has not been reconciled with that literature and the older Allan 1976 'pitch accent' description was not opened.
new_statements.identity_note: Tariku 2010 describes the highland variety (his own 'highland' dialect, which he equates with Hirut's Gok'a dialect); Hirut 2007 describes the Mes'a dialect; Allan 1976 the Jimma dialect (of Gene, Waka, Jimma). All are Dawro proper, glottocode dawr1236 (alt. names Kullo, Konta, Dauro, Dawuro). Glottolog's bookkeeping node gamo1244 'Gamo-Gofa-Dawro' is a separate entry.

new_statements.quote: Allan (1976) writes that pitch normally is non-contrastive, but with some exceptions. Consider the following minimal pairs from Allan (1976), which was later confirmed by Alebachew (2010). The contrast is between high (acute accent) and low (grave accent) pitch. Two examples are shown below: Table 8: Contrastive pitch. bàná - "I will go" / báná - "dust"; dútsà - "part torn off" / dùtsá - "tail". Hirut (2007), on the other hand, does not mention pitch. Alebachew (2010) recounts an unresolved problem of classification in Dawro on whether or not it should be classified as a tonal language or a pitch-accent language. [...] Alebachew (2010) shows that there are grounds to investigate the question of pitch and tone further, but tone has not proven an obstacle during elicitation for the examples in this thesis.

Alebachew (2010) recounts an unresolved problem of classification in Dawro on whether or not it should be classified as a tonal languag…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the existing Tariku 2010 statement (register tone language, two level tones H and L, no stress statement): Hanserud likewise reports an H/L pitch contrast, says nothing about stress, and adds only that Allan 1976 calls the pitch contrast 'normally non-contrastive' and that the tone-vs-pitch accent classification is unresolved (citing Alebachew 2010). It does not name Tariku 2010. No placement of word stress is given, so it neither refines nor contradicts a stress rule; the catalog's empty rule stays empty.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The thesis does not describe word stress at all (the word 'stress' does not occur). Its only word-prosody statement is a second-hand summary: following Allan 1976 and Alebachew 2010, Dawro has a high vs. low pitch contrast that is usually non-contrastive but yields some lexical minimal pairs and two putative grammatical-tone pairs; whether Dawro is a tone language or a pitch accent language is left as an unresolved question, and the author did no phonological analysis of his own. The only other prosodic remarks are about sentence intonation: interrogatives carry a sharp rise in pitch on the interrogative-marked word, described at printed p. 53 as 'a rise on the penultimate syllable of the interrogative-marked verb'.
new_statements.exceptions: Pitch 'normally is non-contrastive, but with some exceptions' (the minimal pairs bàná/báná, dútsà/dùtsá from Allan 1976; grammatical pairs zòʔó/zóʔò 'red/red things', pùnnà/púnná from Alebachew 2010, the latter of which the author doubts because 'blew' should carry a past-tense morpheme). Also notes an unresolved question whether length or tone distinguishes absolutive and accusative forms of a-final nouns (printed p. 25).
new_statements.identity_note: Hanserud 2018 describes Dawro as spoken in the Dawro zone (highland/lowland dialects mentioned at his sec. 1, noting phonological similarity between Wolaitta and the Dawro lowland dialect); his prosody remarks are second-hand from Allan 1976 (Kullo) and Alebachew 2010, not from his own dialect-specific analysis. Same language as the catalog's Dauro/Tariku 2010.

sources.note: Whole thesis is phonology; sec. 3.4 Tone (pp. 58-61) classifies Dauro as a register tone language with two level tones H and L that persist across the whole word, with lexical and grammatical function (minimal pairs k'eesaa/k'éesáa, haitsaa/háitsáa, zoɁo/zóɁó). The word 'stress' is used only generically (p. 44: 'phonological properties like stress and tone take syllable as their domain'); no statement on word stress. sources.note: Sec. 2.3 Tone-accent (pp. 26-29) is about Haro: 'Like other Ometo varieties for which there exist descriptions, such as Wolaitta (Azeb 1996), Zayse (Hayward 1990) and Gamo (Hayward 1994), Haro is a tone-accent language, in which a high tone occurs only once per simple word.' Dawuro is cited for morphology (author's own field notes, Hirut 1999b) but not characterized prosodically.

sources.note: Sec. 1.9.2 Tone (pp. 10-11): reviews Allan (1976:328) 'pitch language' with two levels of systematic pitch (bàná 'I will go' vs báná 'dust'), Hiwot (1988:22) imperative/jussive markers carry high pitch, Hirut (2007:99) last syllable of imperative verb pronounced with high pitch, Siseraw (1989) two tones with most words ending low; concludes Dawro is a tone language (lexical: yédd 'send' vs yèdd 'resign'; grammatical: zòʔó 'red' vs zóʔò 'red things') 'but needs further investigation'. No stress statement.
